newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ, Greenpeace warn against plutonium shipment.
newsitem.headline: NZ, Greenpeace warn against plutonium shipment.

text.p: New Zealand's Foreign Affairs Minister Don McKinnon said on Wednesday the government would seek assurances from Japan that it would not allow a shipment of plutonium waste to pass through New Zealand's exclusive economic zone.
The environmental group Greenpeace said earlier on Wednesday that a shipment of plutonium waste was expected to pass through the Tasman Sea, between Australia and New Zealand, in February.

Greenpeace, citing what it said was a leaked French diplomatic document, said the cargo would contain 40 canisters of plutonium waste encased in glass blocks and carried on the British-registered Pacific Teal to Japan.

The document appeared to have been sent by the French Foreign Ministry in Paris to its embassies in Tokyo, London and Washington, as well as to senior officials in the French nuclear industry, it said.
McKinnon, speaking at a news conference, said: "There will be no doubt in the minds of the Japanese government about the attitudes and concern of the New Zealand government."
"We are concerned. We have made it clear to the Japanese government we do not want this shipment anywhere near New Zealand."
"We recognise of course it can traverse the Tasman (Sea) and not touch...the New Zealand economic zone at all," McKinnon said.
He said New Zealand accepted that Japanese safety requirements for such shipments exceeded current international standards, but Wellington still had concerns about storage and packaging standards.
The waste was produced through reprocessing of Japanese used nuclear fuel into plutonium in France.

Pacific Teal is scheduled to leave France on January 16 and sail via South Africa, Australia and the South Pacific, a route used for a previous shipment in 1992. Another shipment sailed around the southern tip of South America in 1995.

Dr Peter Wills of the Physics Department of the University of Auckland, told a Greenpeace news conference that plutonium created its own heat and if it came in contact with seawater the ocean could become contaminated.
"You would have a large-scale radiological problem if you exposed that to seawater. It would last a long, long period of time," he said.
